title: National income
overview: National income is the total value of goods and services an economy produces, and the total income earned from producing them, over a period of time. This topic introduces the circular flow of income, which is the model behind every later idea in Theme 2 (injections, withdrawals, equilibrium output and the multiplier), and the vital distinction between income (a flow) and wealth (a stock). Examiners reward students who can use the circular flow to trace how a change in one part of the economy spreads to national income as a whole.
objectives: Define national income and explain why output, income and expenditure measures are equal in principle
Distinguish clearly between income (a flow) and wealth (a stock), with examples of each
Draw and explain the two-sector circular flow of income, separating real flows from money flows
Extend the circular flow to include the financial sector, government and the rest of the world
Use the circular flow to analyse how a change in spending affects national income, and evaluate the model's limitations

sections.heading: What national income measures
sections.body:
**National income** is the value of all goods and services produced in an economy over a given period, usually a quarter or a year. Because every pound spent on output becomes a pound of income for someone (wages, rent, interest or profit), the same total can be measured in three ways:

- **Output method**: the value added at each stage of production, summed across all industries. Counting only value added avoids double counting intermediate goods (the flour and the loaf).
- **Income method**: the sum of factor incomes earned in production: wages and salaries, profits, rent and interest.
- **Expenditure method**: total spending on final goods and services, C + I + G + (X − M).

In principle **national output = national income = national expenditure**. In practice the ONS publishes all three and they differ because of measurement errors, so a "statistical discrepancy" is reported.

The main measure is **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**, output produced within the UK's borders. **Gross National Income (GNI)** adds net income from abroad (for example, profits earned by UK firms' overseas subsidiaries minus profits sent home by foreign-owned firms in the UK). UK GDP was roughly £2.8 trillion in current prices in 2024.

Two adjustments matter for the exam. **Nominal** national income is measured at current prices; **real** national income removes the effect of inflation using a price index (the GDP deflator). If nominal GDP rises 6% while prices rise 4%, real GDP has grown by roughly 2%. Economists care about **real** output because only more real goods and services raise living standards. Dividing by population gives national income **per head**, which is the better guide to average living standards.

sections.heading: Income versus wealth
sections.body:
This distinction is examined directly and is a frequent source of lost marks.

- **Income is a flow**: an amount received *per period of time*, such as a salary of £35,000 a year, interest of £400 a year or a pension of £900 a month.
- **Wealth is a stock**: the value of assets owned *at a point in time*, such as a house worth £300,000, shares, savings balances, pension funds or a business. Net wealth = assets minus liabilities (such as a mortgage).

The two are linked. **Wealth generates income**: shares pay dividends, a rented flat pays rent, savings pay interest. **Income builds wealth**: the part of income that is saved adds to the stock of wealth. A household can be income-poor but asset-rich (a retired homeowner) or have a high income but little wealth (a young doctor renting in London).

Why it matters for macroeconomics:

- **The wealth effect.** When house or share prices rise, households feel wealthier and tend to spend a larger share of their income, raising consumption and AD even though income has not changed. Falls in asset prices, as in 2008, have the opposite effect.
- **Inequality.** In the UK wealth is far more unequally distributed than income. ONS data for 2018–2020 suggested the wealthiest tenth of households held over 40% of total household wealth, while the poorest half held less than a tenth. The Gini coefficient for wealth (roughly 0.6) is much higher than for disposable income (roughly 0.35).
- **Policy design.** Most UK taxes fall on income flows (income tax, National Insurance). Taxes on wealth stocks (inheritance tax, council tax, capital gains tax on asset sales) raise far less, which is why debates about "taxing wealth" are separate from debates about income tax.

sections.heading: The two-sector circular flow of income
sections.body:
The **circular flow of income** is a simple model of how money and output move around an economy. Start with only two sectors: **households** and **firms**, and assume households spend all their income on domestic output.

- Households own the factors of production (labour, land, capital, enterprise) and supply **factor services** to firms. This is a **real flow**.
- In return firms pay **factor incomes** (wages, rent, interest, profit). This is a **money flow**, and its total is national income (Y).
- Households spend their income on **goods and services** produced by firms (a real flow) by paying **consumption expenditure** (C), a money flow.

Real flows go one way; money flows go the other. In this closed, two-sector model with no saving, everything earned is spent, so **Y = C** and national income stays constant period after period. Output, income and expenditure are three views of the same flow, which is why the three measurement methods give the same answer.

The key insight is **interdependence**: one person's spending is another person's income. If households cut spending, firms' revenues fall, so firms reduce output and pay less in factor incomes, so households have less to spend. A change in spending at any point in the circle is transmitted all the way round. This is the foundation of the multiplier (2.4.4) and of Keynes's argument that a fall in spending can push an economy into a self-reinforcing recession.

sections.heading: Adding the financial sector, government and the rest of the world
sections.body:
A realistic economy has five sectors. Money can **leak out** of the circular flow or be **injected into** it.

**Withdrawals (leakages)**: income received by households that is not passed on as spending on domestic output.

- **Savings (S)**: income not spent, held in banks or other financial institutions.
- **Taxation (T)**: income tax, National Insurance and VAT paid to government.
- **Imports (M)**: spending on goods and services produced abroad, which becomes income for foreign producers.

**Injections**: spending on domestic output that does not originate from domestic households' consumption.

- **Investment (I)**: firms' spending on capital goods, often financed by the financial sector out of savings.
- **Government spending (G)**: spending on public services and capital projects (the NHS, schools, roads). Note that transfer payments such as Universal Credit are not part of G, because no output is produced in exchange.
- **Exports (X)**: spending by foreigners on UK-produced goods and services.

The financial sector links S and I, the government links T and G, and the rest of the world links M and X. Crucially, the people who save are not the people who invest, and their decisions are made for different reasons, so there is no automatic reason for withdrawals to equal injections. That mismatch is what makes national income rise or fall, which is developed in 2.4.2.

sections.heading: Using the circular flow in analysis, and its limitations
sections.body:
The circular flow lets you trace the effect of any shock on national income in a logical chain, which is exactly what analysis marks reward. For example: a fall in consumer confidence → households save more (S rises) → spending on domestic output falls → firms' revenues fall → firms cut output and employment → factor incomes fall → national income falls.

The model has limitations, which can be used as evaluation:

- **It is static and simplified.** It does not show the price level, so it cannot tell you whether a rise in spending raises real output or just causes inflation. AD/AS analysis (2.4.3) is needed for that.
- **Leakages are not lost for ever.** Savings deposited in banks may be lent to firms for investment; tax revenue funds government spending; import spending may return as demand for UK exports. The net effect depends on how quickly and fully leakages are recycled.
- **Expectations and confidence** drive saving and investment decisions in ways the diagram does not capture.
- **Measurement problems**: the hidden economy, unpaid work (caring, volunteering) and quality changes are not fully captured in national income statistics, so the "size" of the flow is an estimate subject to revision.

key_terms.definition: The total value of goods and services produced in an economy in a given period, equal in principle to total factor incomes earned and to total expenditure on final output.
The total value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a period, usually a year or a quarter.
GDP plus net income from abroad: income earned by residents from overseas assets minus income paid to foreign owners of domestic assets.
A flow of money received over a period of time, such as wages, rent, interest, dividends or profit.
A stock of assets owned at a point in time, such as property, shares, savings and pension funds; net wealth deducts liabilities.

A model showing the flow of factor services, goods and services, and the matching money flows of income and expenditure between households and firms (and, in the extended model, financial institutions, government and the rest of the world).
A flow of factors of production or goods and services between sectors, moving in the opposite direction to the corresponding money flow.
Income that is not passed on as spending on domestic output: savings, taxation and imports.
Spending on domestic output that does not come from domestic households' consumption: investment, government spending and exports.
The tendency for consumer spending to rise when the value of households' assets (such as housing or shares) rises, and to fall when asset values fall.
National income adjusted for changes in the price level, so that it measures changes in the volume of output.

diagrams.title: Two-sector circular flow of income
diagrams.x: Schematic: money flows solid, real flows dashed
diagrams.caption: Households supply factor services to firms and receive factor incomes (Y); they spend that income on firms' goods and services (C). Real flows (dashed) move opposite to money flows (solid). With no leakages, Y = C and national income is constant.

formulae.name: Expenditure measure of national income
formulae.formula: Y = C + I + G + (X − M)

formulae.name: Real national income
formulae.formula: Real GDP = Nominal GDP × (Base-year price index ÷ Current price index)
formulae.example: Nominal GDP £2,400bn, price index 120 (base year = 100): real GDP = 2,400 × 100/120 = £2,000bn at base-year prices.

formulae.name: Approximate real growth
formulae.formula: Real growth (%) ≈ nominal growth (%) − inflation (%)
formulae.example: Nominal GDP up 6%, GDP deflator up 4%: real growth ≈ 2%.

applications: UK housing wealth and consumption: because most UK household wealth is held in property and pensions, movements in house prices feed through to spending. Rising house prices in the 2000s encouraged mortgage equity withdrawal, boosting consumption; the fall in house prices in 2008–09 contributed to the sharp drop in consumer spending during the financial crisis.

The 2020 lockdowns show circular-flow interdependence: when households were prevented from spending on hospitality and travel, firms' revenues collapsed and their ability to pay factor incomes fell. The Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (furlough), which paid 80% of the wages of furloughed workers, was designed to keep the income flow to households going so that the fall in spending would not spiral further.

Ireland illustrates why the choice of measure matters: GDP has been heavily inflated by the profits of multinational firms booked there, so Irish GDP overstates the income actually available to Irish residents. The Irish authorities publish a modified GNI measure (GNI*) to give a truer picture.

Income versus wealth in UK policy: debates about taxing wealth (such as reforming capital gains tax, inheritance tax or council tax bands that still reflect 1991 property values in England) are about stocks, while income tax and National Insurance rates are about flows; they affect different households and have different effects on spending.
evaluation: The circular flow cannot show whether higher spending raises real output or only prices; that depends on spare capacity, so always link to AD/AS and the position relative to full capacity.

Leakages are not necessarily lost: savings may be recycled into investment through banks, and tax into government spending. The net effect on national income depends on how much and how quickly withdrawals are re-injected.

The strength of the wealth effect depends on whether gains are seen as permanent and on how easily households can borrow against them; after 2008 tighter mortgage lending weakened the link between house prices and spending.

Equal measures of output, income and expenditure hold only in principle; data are estimated, revised and miss the hidden economy and unpaid work, so judgements based on small changes in national income should be cautious.
Higher GDP is not the same as higher living standards: per-head figures, distribution of income and wealth, and non-market factors (leisure, environment) all matter.
misconceptions: Saying 'income and wealth are the same thing'. Income is a flow per period; wealth is a stock at a point in time. A house is wealth; the rent from it is income.
Including transfer payments (state pensions, Universal Credit) in government spending G. They are transfers of income, not payment for output, so they are excluded from G in the expenditure measure.
Thinking a withdrawal always reduces national income. National income falls only if total withdrawals exceed total injections; savings re-lent for investment do not reduce it.
Confusing nominal and real GDP. A rise in nominal GDP can occur with no rise, or a fall, in real output if inflation is high enough.
Drawing the circular flow with real and money flows going in the same direction. They always move in opposite directions.
exam_tips: Short-answer questions often ask you to distinguish income from wealth; give a definition of each, the flow/stock distinction and a UK example of each to secure all marks.

When explaining any change in national income, build a chain round the circular flow: spending → firms' revenue → output and employment → factor incomes → further spending. Each link is an analysis mark.
Use 'real' and 'nominal' precisely. If a data extract gives nominal figures and inflation, calculate the approximate real change; examiners reward this application.
For evaluation, question whether leakages are permanent and whether extra spending increases output or prices.
Draw the circular flow neatly with clear labels if asked; you may add the three withdrawals and three injections to show the extended model.

model_answer.question: Examine how a significant rise in UK house prices might affect national income. Refer to the distinction between income and wealth in your answer.
model_answer.answer:
National income is the total value of output produced in the economy over a period, equal in principle to total factor incomes and total spending. Income is a flow received per period, such as wages, whereas wealth is a stock of assets held at a point in time, such as a house. A rise in house prices does not directly change national income, because no new output is produced when an existing house rises in value; it increases the wealth of homeowners.

However, higher wealth can affect national income indirectly through the wealth effect. Homeowners who see the value of their main asset rise feel more financially secure, so they save a smaller proportion of their income and their consumption rises. Some may borrow against the extra equity by remortgaging to fund home improvements or cars. Because consumption makes up over 60% of UK aggregate demand, even a modest fall in the savings ratio can raise AD noticeably. In circular-flow terms, the withdrawal of savings falls while injections are unchanged, so spending on domestic output rises; firms' revenues rise, they increase output and employment, and the extra factor incomes are spent again, so national income rises by more than the initial increase in spending. Rising house prices also raise the value of collateral, so banks may be more willing to lend, adding further to spending. Construction may increase too, as new-build homes become more profitable, which is an injection of investment.

The size of the effect is uncertain. First, the gain in wealth is concentrated among older homeowners, who may have a lower propensity to spend, while renters and first-time buyers become relatively worse off, since they must save more for a deposit; their consumption could fall, offsetting part of the effect. Second, since 2008 mortgage lending rules have been tighter, so households cannot borrow against housing equity as easily as in the early 2000s, weakening the link. Third, a share of any extra spending leaks into imports, especially consumer durables, so the boost to UK national income is smaller than the rise in spending. Finally, if the economy is close to full capacity, higher spending is likely to raise the price level rather than real national income.

Overall, a rise in house prices is likely to raise national income modestly in the short run through the wealth effect and higher construction, but the effect depends critically on households' confidence that the gains are permanent, on credit conditions and on spare capacity. It is a less reliable source of growth than higher productive investment.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of national income, income and wealth, with the flow/stock distinction used to make the key point that asset price rises are not output. Application: UK context (consumption share of AD, post-2008 lending rules, imports). Analysis: two developed chains (wealth effect via consumption and collateral; construction investment) linked to the circular flow and multiplied effect. Evaluation: distributional offset, credit conditions, import leakage and spare capacity, ending with a supported judgement that the effect is modest and conditional. This would reach the top level for an 8-mark question.

check.q: Which of the following is an example of wealth rather than income?
options: Monthly state pension of £900
Dividends of £300 received this year
Portfolio of shares valued at £40,000 today
Annual rent of £9,000 received from a tenant
check.explanation: Wealth is a stock of assets at a point in time. The share portfolio is a stock; the pension, dividends and rent are flows of income per period.

check.q: In the circular flow of income, which of the following is an injection?
options: Spending by UK households on imported cars
Income tax paid by workers
Spending by German tourists in London
Interest-bearing deposits in UK banks
check.explanation: Spending by foreigners on UK output is an export, an injection. Imports, taxes and savings are withdrawals.

check.q: Nominal GDP rises by 5% and the GDP deflator rises by 3%. What is the approximate change in real GDP?
options: Rise of 8%
Rise of 2%
Fall of 2%
Rise of 1.67%
check.explanation: Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation: 5% − 3% = 2%.

check.q: Why are Universal Credit payments excluded from government spending (G) when measuring national income by the expenditure method?
options: They are financed by borrowing
They are transfer payments, not payment for currently produced output
They are paid only to unemployed people
They are counted as investment instead
check.explanation: Transfer payments redistribute income without any good or service being produced in return; including them would overstate output. They affect national income only when recipients spend them.

title: Injections and withdrawals
overview: Injections (investment, government spending and exports) add spending to the circular flow, while withdrawals (saving, taxation and imports) drain it. When injections exceed withdrawals national income rises; when withdrawals exceed injections it falls, until the two are brought back into balance by the change in income itself. This topic explains why national income settles where it does and underpins the multiplier, fiscal policy and the paradox of thrift.
objectives: Identify each injection and withdrawal and explain what determines it
Explain why national income is in equilibrium when total injections equal total withdrawals
Analyse how a change in an injection or a withdrawal changes national income, using the circular flow and AD/AS
Calculate equilibrium national income from simple data on injections and withdrawal propensities
Evaluate the paradox of thrift and the importance of sector balances for the UK economy

sections.heading: The three injections and what drives them
sections.body:
An **injection** is spending on domestic output that does not come from domestic households' consumption out of their current income. Injections are largely **autonomous**: they are determined by factors other than the current level of domestic national income.

- **Investment (I)**: spending by firms on capital goods such as machinery, buildings and software, plus new housing. It depends on interest rates (the cost of borrowing and the opportunity cost of retained profit), business confidence ('animal spirits'), expected demand (the accelerator), technology, corporation tax and capital allowances such as full expensing, and access to credit.
- **Government spending (G)**: current spending on public services (NHS staff wages, schools) and capital spending (roads, rail, hospitals). It depends on political choices, fiscal rules and the state of the economy. Transfer payments are excluded.
- **Exports (X)**: spending by overseas residents on UK goods and services. They depend on income in trading partners (the US and EU), the sterling exchange rate, relative inflation and productivity (competitiveness), and trade barriers.

Because injections are driven mainly by outside forces, a change in any one of them is a common starting point for a shock to the economy: an export collapse when the world goes into recession, a cut in investment when confidence falls, or a rise in G in an expansionary budget.

sections.heading: The three withdrawals and what drives them
sections.body:
A **withdrawal** (leakage) is any part of income that is not passed on as spending on domestic output.

- **Saving (S)**: income not spent. It depends on interest rates, confidence and precautionary motives, expectations of future income, wealth and demographics. The UK household saving ratio has been as low as around 4–5% of disposable income in some years and briefly rose above 25% in 2020 when lockdown removed opportunities to spend.
- **Taxation (T)**: direct taxes on income (income tax, National Insurance) and indirect taxes on spending (VAT, excise duties). Revenue depends on tax rates and on the level of income and spending.
- **Imports (M)**: spending on foreign goods and services. It depends on domestic income, the exchange rate, relative prices and the quality and availability of foreign products. The UK has a high propensity to import, with imports equal to roughly a third of GDP.

The crucial feature is that **all three withdrawals rise as national income rises**. When households earn more they save more, pay more tax (especially under progressive income tax) and buy more imports. This is what makes the system self-correcting: changes in income change withdrawals until they match injections again. The fraction of each extra pound of income that is withdrawn is the **marginal propensity to withdraw (MPW)** = MPS + MPT + MPM, which determines the size of the multiplier (2.4.4).

sections.heading: Equilibrium: why injections equal withdrawals
sections.body:
National income is in **equilibrium** when there is no tendency for it to change. In the circular flow, this occurs when **total injections equal total withdrawals: I + G + X = S + T + M**.

- If **J > W**, more is being added to the flow than is leaking out. Spending on domestic output exceeds the value of current output, firms' stocks run down, and firms expand output and employment. National income **rises**. As it rises, S, T and M all rise, until W has increased to equal J.
- If **W > J**, more leaks out than is put in. Spending falls short of output, unsold stocks build up, firms cut production and jobs, and national income **falls**. As income falls, S, T and M fall, until W has fallen to equal J.

Note that it is **total** injections and **total** withdrawals that must be equal, not each pair. The UK can have S > I, T < G and M > X at the same time; these sector balances simply have to sum to zero in equilibrium.

**Worked example (illustrative data).** Suppose I = £200bn, G = £300bn and X = £250bn, so J = £750bn. Households save 10p, pay 25p in tax and spend 15p on imports out of every £1 of income, so W = 0.5Y. Equilibrium requires 0.5Y = 750, so **Y = £1,500bn**. If exports rise by £50bn, J = £800bn and the new equilibrium is Y = 800 ÷ 0.5 = **£1,600bn**. A £50bn injection has raised national income by £100bn: this is the multiplier at work (k = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2).

sections.heading: Linking injections and withdrawals to AD/AS
sections.body:
AD = C + I + G + (X − M), so injections and withdrawals map directly on to aggregate demand.

- A rise in an injection (I, G or X) shifts **AD to the right**.
- A rise in the propensity to withdraw (households save more out of each pound, a tax rise, or a switch towards imports) reduces C or raises M, shifting **AD to the left**.

On an AD/AS diagram, the effect on real output and the price level depends on the slope of SRAS and how close the economy is to full capacity. With spare capacity, a rise in injections mainly raises real national output and employment; near full capacity, it mainly raises the price level.

The AD/AS approach adds what the circular flow lacks: the price level. A rise in injections that pushes the economy beyond its productive potential creates demand-pull inflation rather than lasting real growth. This is why the Bank of England watches the balance of spending against capacity when setting Bank Rate.

sections.heading: The paradox of thrift and sector balances
sections.body:
Keynes highlighted the **paradox of thrift**: if all households try to save more at the same time, total saving may not rise at all. Higher planned saving raises withdrawals above injections, so national income falls; as income falls, households' ability to save falls too, so actual saving ends up roughly where it started, but at a lower level of income and employment. What is sensible for one household (saving for a rainy day) can be damaging for the economy as a whole, a classic **fallacy of composition**.

Evaluate this carefully:

- If higher saving is channelled by banks into higher **investment** (for example because interest rates fall), withdrawals are recycled into injections and national income need not fall; in the long run more investment raises productive capacity.
- The paradox is most relevant in a recession, when firms do not want to invest whatever the interest rate, and when interest rates are already close to zero, as after 2008 and in 2020.
- Over the long run, low national saving can be a problem: the UK has long had relatively low saving and investment and a persistent current account deficit, financed by borrowing from abroad or by selling assets to overseas buyers.

**Sector balances** follow from the equilibrium condition: (S − I) + (T − G) + (M − X) = 0. If the government runs a deficit (G > T) and the country runs a trade deficit (M > X), the private sector must be saving more than it invests. This framework is useful when evaluating fiscal austerity: if the government cuts its deficit, either the private sector must save less, or the trade balance must improve, or national income will fall until the identity holds.

key_terms.definition: Spending on domestic output that does not originate from domestic households' consumption: investment (I), government spending (G) and exports (X).
Any part of income not passed on in the circular flow as spending on domestic output: saving (S), taxation (T) and imports (M).
Spending that does not depend on the current level of national income, such as most investment, government spending and exports.
The level of national income at which total injections equal total withdrawals, so there is no tendency for income to rise or fall.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that is withdrawn from the circular flow: MPS + MPT + MPM.
Household saving as a percentage of household disposable income.
The idea that if all households attempt to save more at once, national income falls and total saving may not rise, so an action rational for individuals harms the economy as a whole.
The mistaken belief that what is true for an individual must be true for the whole economy.
The identity (S − I) + (T − G) + (M − X) = 0, showing that the private, government and overseas sector surpluses and deficits must sum to zero.

diagrams.title: Five-sector circular flow: withdrawals and injections
diagrams.caption: Saving, taxation and imports leak out of the household income flow to the financial sector, government and rest of the world; investment, government spending and exports are injected back into spending on firms' output. National income is in equilibrium when I + G + X = S + T + M.

diagrams.title: Injections exceed withdrawals: AD shifts right
diagrams.caption: A rise in injections (for example higher exports) or a fall in the propensity to withdraw shifts AD from AD1 to AD2. Real output rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level from P1 to P2; the split between the two depends on spare capacity.

formulae.name: Equilibrium condition
formulae.formula: I + G + X = S + T + M  (J = W)

formulae.name: Marginal propensity to withdraw
formulae.formula: MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM = ΔW ÷ ΔY
formulae.example: Out of an extra £100 of income, £10 is saved, £20 taxed and £15 spent on imports: MPW = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.45.

formulae.name: Sector balances
formulae.example: If the government deficit is £80bn (T − G = −80) and the trade deficit is £30bn (M − X = 30), the private sector surplus must be S − I = £50bn.

applications: Export injections and the world economy: when global trade collapsed in 2008–09, UK exports fell sharply even though sterling depreciated by roughly a quarter, showing that foreign income can matter more than the exchange rate for this injection.

The 2020 surge in household saving: with shops, travel and hospitality closed, the UK household saving ratio jumped to more than 25% of disposable income in mid-2020. This huge rise in withdrawals, alongside falling investment and exports, contributed to the roughly 10% fall in UK real GDP in 2020, while a large increase in government spending (furlough, business support) partly offset it.

Investment incentives: the introduction of full expensing in 2023 (allowing companies to deduct the full cost of qualifying plant and machinery from taxable profits in the year of purchase) aimed to raise the investment injection, which has been weak in the UK relative to other G7 economies for many years.

Germany and China have run large current account surpluses (X > M) for long periods, while the UK and US have run persistent deficits. Sector balances show that a country with a trade deficit needs either private saving above investment or a government deficit to finance it.
evaluation: The effect of a change in an injection on real national income depends on spare capacity: with a negative output gap it mainly raises output and employment; near full capacity it mainly raises inflation.

Withdrawals may be recycled: saving deposited with banks may finance investment and tax revenue finances government spending, so the net effect of a rise in a withdrawal is smaller than a simple model implies. How much is recycled depends on confidence and interest rates.

Injections and withdrawals are interdependent. Higher exports raise income and therefore imports; higher government spending may be financed by higher taxes, so a balanced-budget change is far less expansionary than a debt-financed one.

The paradox of thrift is most powerful in a deep recession with interest rates near zero; in normal times, higher saving can lower interest rates and raise investment, and in the long run more saving funds capital accumulation and potential growth.
Time lags: changes in income take several quarters to work through, and the equilibrium may never be reached because injections keep changing.
misconceptions: Thinking that equilibrium requires S = I, T = G and X = M separately. Only total injections must equal total withdrawals.
Treating a budget deficit as automatically a withdrawal. A deficit means G exceeds T: on balance the government is injecting more than it withdraws.
Saying saving is always bad for the economy. Saving finances investment; the paradox of thrift applies when saving is not recycled into investment.
Forgetting that withdrawals depend on income. It is the change in income that brings withdrawals back into line with injections.
exam_tips: If asked why national income changes, state the J vs W comparison, then build the chain: firms' stocks, output, employment, incomes and the induced change in S, T and M.
Calculation questions may give injections and withdrawal propensities; set J = MPW × Y and solve. Show the working clearly for method marks.
Use the sector-balances identity in data-response answers on the budget deficit or current account; it impresses examiners when used accurately.
For evaluation, always ask whether withdrawals are recycled, whether the economy has spare capacity, and how big the change is relative to GDP.

model_answer.question: UK household saving rose sharply in 2020. Using the concepts of injections and withdrawals, examine the likely impact of a rise in household saving on UK national income.
model_answer.answer:
Saving is a withdrawal from the circular flow of income because it is income that is not spent on domestic output. Injections are spending on domestic output not originating from households' current consumption: investment, government spending and exports. National income is in equilibrium when total injections equal total withdrawals; if withdrawals rise above injections, national income falls until the two are again equal.

A rise in household saving, for example because households are worried about losing their jobs, means that for any given level of income consumption is lower. Withdrawals now exceed injections. Firms find that spending on their output has fallen, so unsold stocks build up and they cut production and employment. The workers who lose jobs or hours receive less factor income and cut their own spending, so firms elsewhere lose revenue too. National income falls by a multiple of the initial fall in consumption. As incomes fall, households save less in absolute terms, pay less tax and buy fewer imports, so withdrawals fall until they equal injections at a lower equilibrium. On an AD/AS diagram, AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2, reducing real output from Y1 to Y2 and lowering the price level or the rate of inflation.

This creates the paradox of thrift. If all households try to save more, national income falls, and because saving depends on income, total saving may end up no higher than before. Each household acts rationally but the collective result is lower income and employment.

However, the impact depends on several factors. First, whether savings are recycled: if banks lend the extra deposits to firms, and lower interest rates encourage investment, the rise in withdrawals is matched by a rise in injections and national income need not fall. In 2020 this recycling was weak because firms faced extreme uncertainty, but the Bank of England cut Bank Rate to 0.1% and expanded quantitative easing to support lending. Second, government spending: in 2020 the government greatly increased G and transfers through furlough and business support, injecting spending that offset much of the fall in consumption, and running a large deficit that absorbed private saving. Third, the cause of the saving matters: in 2020 much saving was 'forced' because shops and travel were closed rather than chosen, so it was released as spending once restrictions ended, contributing to strong demand in 2021. Finally, part of the fall in consumption reduces imports rather than UK output, so the fall in UK national income is smaller than the rise in saving suggests.

Overall, a rise in household saving is likely to reduce national income in the short run, especially when investment is weak and interest rates are already low. But the size and duration of the fall depend on whether withdrawals are recycled into injections and on the government's response; the 2020 rise in saving was largely temporary, so its long-run effect on national income was limited.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate definitions of injections, withdrawals and equilibrium. Application: UK 2020 context (Bank Rate, QE, furlough, forced saving). Analysis: a full chain from higher saving through firms' output, employment and income to a new equilibrium, linked to AD/AS and the paradox of thrift. Evaluation: four distinct, well-developed points (recycling of saving, government injections, cause of saving, import leakage) and a judgement weighing short-run against long-run effects. This meets the Level 3/Level 4 descriptors for a 10-mark question.

title: Equilibrium real national output
overview: Macroeconomic equilibrium is the level of real national output and the price level at which aggregate demand equals aggregate supply. This topic is where AD/AS analysis comes together: you must be able to show equilibrium, show how shifts in AD and AS change real output and the price level, distinguish movements along curves from shifts, and contrast the Keynesian and classical views of long-run aggregate supply. Almost every Theme 2 essay relies on these diagrams.
objectives: Draw and explain macroeconomic equilibrium using AD, SRAS and LRAS
Distinguish between a movement along and a shift of the AD and AS curves
Analyse the effect of shifts in AD and in SRAS on real output, the price level and employment
Compare the Keynesian and classical (free market) views of LRAS and the long-run adjustment process
Evaluate the effect of a shock by considering the slope of AS, spare capacity, the size of the shift and time

sections.heading: Equilibrium where AD meets AS
sections.body:
**Aggregate demand (AD)** is total planned spending on an economy's goods and services at each price level: AD = C + I + G + (X − M). It slopes downward because a lower price level raises the real value of wealth (wealth effect), makes UK goods more competitive against foreign goods (international trade effect) and, through lower demand for money, tends to reduce interest rates (interest rate effect).

**Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS)** is the total output firms plan to supply at each price level, assuming factor prices (especially money wages) are fixed. It slopes upward because, with costs fixed in the short run, a higher price level raises profitability of extra output and firms face rising marginal costs as they use capacity more intensively.

**Macroeconomic equilibrium** occurs where AD = SRAS, giving the equilibrium **price level** and **real national output**. At any higher price level, planned supply exceeds planned demand, unsold stocks build up, and firms cut output and prices. At any lower price level, demand exceeds supply, stocks run down, and firms raise output and prices. The economy is pulled towards the intersection.

**Real** national output means output measured at constant prices, so a rise represents more goods and services, not just higher prices. The level of employment is closely related: firms need more labour to produce more output, so a rise in equilibrium real output usually reduces unemployment (it is a derived demand).

sections.heading: Movements along versus shifts of the curves
sections.body:
This distinction earns marks and avoids serious errors.

- A **movement along AD** is caused only by a change in the **price level**. A rise in the price level reduces the quantity of real output demanded; this is a contraction along AD, not a shift.
- A **shift in AD** is caused by a change in any component of AD at a given price level: consumer confidence, interest rates, wealth, government spending, taxes, the exchange rate, foreign incomes, business expectations. Right is an increase, left a decrease.
- A **movement along SRAS** is again caused only by a change in the price level, typically following a shift in AD.
- A **shift in SRAS** is caused by a change in firms' **costs of production** at every level of output: money wages, raw material and energy prices, import prices (affected by the exchange rate), indirect taxes and subsidies, and short-run productivity changes. Higher costs shift SRAS **left (up)**; lower costs shift it **right (down)**.
- A **shift in LRAS** is caused by a change in the **quantity or quality of factors of production**: labour force size and skills, capital stock, technology, institutions and incentives (2.3.3).

A common exam trap is a question about a fall in the exchange rate. This shifts AD right (exports cheaper, imports dearer) but also shifts SRAS left (imported raw materials cost more). A strong answer shows both and explains which effect is likely to dominate.

sections.heading: Shifts in AD: demand-side shocks
sections.body:
Suppose consumer confidence rises, or the government increases spending. AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. At the original price level there is now excess demand, so firms expand output (a movement along SRAS) and the price level rises.

**Results:** real output rises (Y1 to Y2), the price level rises (P1 to P2), unemployment falls. This is the pattern of **demand-pull inflation** combined with growth.

How much of the shift goes into output and how much into prices depends on the **slope of SRAS**, which reflects **spare capacity**:

- With large spare capacity (a deep negative output gap), firms can hire unemployed workers and use idle machines at little extra cost, so SRAS is flat: mostly output rises.
- Close to full capacity, firms compete for scarce labour and materials, costs rise steeply, SRAS is steep: mostly prices rise.

A fall in AD has the opposite effects: lower real output, higher unemployment and a lower price level (in practice, usually a lower rate of inflation rather than falling prices, because wages and prices are 'sticky' downwards). The 2008–09 fall in AD is a clear UK example: real GDP fell by around 6% from peak to trough and unemployment rose to over 8%.

sections.heading: Shifts in SRAS: supply-side shocks
sections.body:
Suppose world energy prices rise sharply. Firms' costs rise at every level of output, so SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. At the original price level, there is excess demand; the price level rises, which causes a contraction along AD.

**Results:** the price level rises (P1 to P2) **and** real output falls (Y1 to Y2), so unemployment rises. This combination is **stagflation**, produced by **cost-push inflation**. It is especially difficult for policymakers because the two main objectives conflict: raising interest rates to fight inflation deepens the fall in output, while boosting demand to protect output adds to inflation (2.6.4).

A favourable supply shock, such as a fall in oil prices or a rise in productivity, shifts SRAS right: the price level falls (or inflation slows) and real output rises at the same time, the best of both worlds.

The impact of a supply shock depends on the **slope of AD** and on whether the shock is **temporary or permanent**. A temporary rise in import prices may reverse; a permanent loss of productive capacity, for example from new trade barriers that reduce efficiency, would also shift LRAS left.

sections.heading: Long-run equilibrium: Keynesian and classical views
sections.body:
Economists disagree about how the economy behaves in the long run, and the Edexcel specification requires both views.

**Classical (free market) view.** LRAS is **vertical** at the full-employment level of output (Yfe), determined by the economy's productive capacity, not by the price level. If AD rises, the short-run equilibrium moves beyond Yfe; the labour market is tight, so workers demand and win higher money wages. Higher costs shift SRAS left until the economy returns to Yfe at a **higher price level**. In the long run, demand-side policy changes only prices. Equally, after a fall in AD, wages and prices fall and the economy returns to full employment on its own; government intervention is unnecessary and may be harmful.

**Keynesian view.** The LRAS curve has three ranges. At low output there is massive spare capacity, so it is **horizontal**: more demand raises output with no rise in prices. In the middle range bottlenecks appear and both output and prices rise. At full capacity (Yfe) the curve becomes **vertical**: more demand raises only prices. Crucially, Keynes argued that wages are sticky downwards and that confidence can collapse, so the economy can be stuck in equilibrium well below full employment for a long time. As he put it in essence, in the long run we are all dead: waiting for self-correction is too costly, so active demand management is justified.

Which view is right? The evidence suggests it depends on circumstances. The prolonged unemployment of the 1930s and the slow recovery after 2008 fit the Keynesian view; the rapid rise in inflation in 2021–22 when demand recovered against constrained supply fits the classical warning that pushing demand beyond capacity creates inflation.

sections.heading: Evaluating AD/AS outcomes
sections.body:
To turn an AD/AS diagram into Level 3 evaluation, ask:

- **Where is the economy relative to full capacity?** The same AD shift has very different effects in a recession and a boom.
- **How large is the shift?** A rise in G worth 0.1% of GDP will barely move the curve; compare the size of the change to total GDP.
- **Is there a multiplier?** An initial AD shift will be amplified (2.4.4), but leakages, especially the UK's high propensity to import, weaken this.
- **Do both curves shift?** Many real events affect both AD and AS: a depreciation, a rise in the National Living Wage (higher costs and higher consumer incomes), or capital investment (raises AD now and LRAS later).
- **Time period.** Short-run effects can be reversed in the long run as wages and expectations adjust (classical view), or persist (Keynesian view).
- **Confidence and expectations**, which can amplify or dampen any shock.

key_terms.definition: The level of real national output and the price level at which aggregate demand equals aggregate supply.
Total planned spending on an economy's goods and services at each possible price level in a given period: C + I + G + (X − M).
Total planned output at each price level when factor prices, especially money wages, are held constant.
The productive potential of the economy when all factors are fully and efficiently employed; determined by the quantity and quality of factors of production.
A sustained rise in the price level caused by aggregate demand growing faster than the economy's capacity to supply.
A sustained rise in the price level caused by rising costs of production, shifting SRAS to the left.
The combination of rising inflation with stagnant or falling real output and rising unemployment, typically caused by an adverse supply shock.
An unexpected event that changes firms' costs or productive capacity, shifting SRAS (and possibly LRAS).
The level of real output at which all resources are fully employed, given by the vertical LRAS in the classical view.
Unused resources (unemployed labour, idle capital) in an economy producing below its potential output.

diagrams.title: Increase in AD with upward-sloping SRAS
diagrams.caption: A rise in AD (AD1 to AD2) raises real output from Y1 to Y2 and the price level from P1 to P2: growth with demand-pull inflation, and lower unemployment.

diagrams.title: Adverse supply shock: SRAS shifts left
diagrams.caption: Higher energy or import costs shift SRAS left. The price level rises from P1 to P2 while real output falls from Y1 to Y2: cost-push inflation and stagflation.

diagrams.title: Keynesian AS: effect of AD depends on spare capacity
diagrams.caption: AD1 to AD2 (horizontal range): output rises, prices unchanged. AD2 to AD3 (intermediate range): output and prices both rise. AD3 to AD4 (near-vertical range at Yfe): a large rise in prices for little extra output.

diagrams.title: Classical long-run adjustment to higher AD
diagrams.caption: Higher AD moves the economy from E1 to E2, above full employment. Tight labour markets raise money wages, shifting SRAS1 to SRAS2; the economy returns to Yfe at E3 with a permanently higher price level.

applications: 2021–22 UK inflation: demand recovered strongly after lockdowns (AD right) while global supply chains, labour shortages and then the surge in gas prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine shifted SRAS left. CPI inflation reached 11.1% in October 2022, a 41-year high, while growth slowed sharply: a textbook mix of demand-pull and cost-push forces.

Energy Price Guarantee: from October 2022 the government capped the unit price of household energy so that a typical household's annual bill was limited to about £2,500. This reduced the measured rise in the price level (limiting the cost-push effect on CPI) and protected household real incomes and consumption, at a large fiscal cost.

The 2008–09 recession: falling house prices, the banking crisis and collapsing confidence shifted AD sharply left. UK real GDP fell by around 6% from peak to trough and unemployment rose from about 5% to over 8%, while inflation fell. The slow recovery and persistent spare capacity are consistent with the Keynesian view.

1970s oil shocks: the quadrupling of oil prices in 1973–74 shifted SRAS left across the developed world, producing stagflation. UK inflation peaked at over 20% in 1975 while unemployment rose, undermining faith in simple demand management.
evaluation: The effect of an AD shift depends on spare capacity and the slope of SRAS/LRAS; always say where the economy starts relative to full capacity, using output gap or unemployment data if given.
Many shocks shift more than one curve (for example a depreciation, minimum wage rises or capital investment), so the net effect on output and prices is ambiguous and depends on relative magnitudes.

Time matters: classical economists expect the economy to return to full employment as wages adjust, but Keynesians argue sticky wages and weak confidence can leave the economy below capacity for years.
Size of the shock relative to GDP: a change of a few billion pounds is small against UK GDP of roughly £2.8 trillion.
AD/AS is a simplification: it compresses expectations, financial conditions and global factors into curves, and the curves themselves cannot be observed directly.
misconceptions: Shifting AD because the price level changed. A change in the price level causes a movement along AD, not a shift.
Shifting LRAS for a change in costs such as oil prices. Changes in costs shift SRAS; LRAS shifts only if productive capacity changes.
Assuming a rise in AD always causes inflation. With a large negative output gap (Keynesian horizontal range) output can rise with little effect on prices.
Forgetting the price level falls in the diagram when AD shifts left. In reality this usually shows as lower inflation rather than deflation, which you should explain.
Mixing up the axes: the vertical axis is the price level, not price; the horizontal axis is real national output, not quantity.
exam_tips: Label every diagram fully: axes (Price level, Real national output), curves (AD1, AD2, SRAS, LRAS), original and new equilibria, P1/P2 and Y1/Y2. Refer to the labels in your writing.
For 'discuss the effects' questions, state the impact on all four key variables where relevant: real output (growth), price level (inflation), unemployment and, often, the current account.
Use the Keynesian AS curve when the question gives clues about spare capacity (high unemployment, recession) and the classical model when discussing long-run effects.
For evaluation, consider whether more than one curve shifts and which effect dominates; examiners reward this two-sided analysis.
Link to data: if an extract shows inflation rising and GDP falling together, identify a supply-side shock.

model_answer.question: Discuss the likely effects of a sharp and sustained rise in world energy prices on UK real national output and the price level. Use an AD/AS diagram in your answer.
model_answer.answer:
Macroeconomic equilibrium is where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply, which determines real national output and the price level. Energy is an input for almost all firms (for heating, transport and manufacturing processes), so a sharp rise in world energy prices increases costs of production at every level of output. This shifts the SRAS curve to the left, from SRAS1 to SRAS2. At the original price level P1 there is now excess demand, so the price level rises to P2, causing a contraction along AD, and real output falls from Y1 to Y2. The result is cost-push inflation combined with lower output and higher unemployment: stagflation.

There are further effects through AD. The UK is a net importer of energy, so higher energy prices transfer income abroad. Households must spend more on gas, electricity and petrol, so their real disposable income falls and spending on other goods and services is reduced. Firms facing squeezed profit margins and uncertainty may postpone investment. These effects shift AD to the left as well, reinforcing the fall in real output, though moderating the rise in the price level. There may also be second-round effects: if workers bargain for higher money wages to restore their real incomes, firms' costs rise again and SRAS shifts further left, creating a wage-price spiral.

This was broadly the UK's experience in 2022, when gas prices rose to several times their previous levels after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. CPI inflation reached 11.1% in October 2022, while real GDP growth slowed to close to zero in 2023.

The size of the effects depends on several factors. First, the energy intensity of the economy: the UK is service-dominated, so energy is a smaller share of costs than in a heavy-manufacturing economy, and the SRAS shift is smaller. Second, the government response: the Energy Price Guarantee, which limited typical household bills to around £2,500 a year, cut the measured rise in the price level and supported real incomes, limiting the fall in AD, though at a fiscal cost of tens of billions of pounds. Third, the Bank of England's response: by raising Bank Rate from 0.1% to 5.25% between December 2021 and August 2023, the MPC limited second-round effects and anchored inflation expectations, but at the cost of further reducing AD and output in the short run. Fourth, whether the rise is temporary: if energy prices fall back, SRAS shifts back to the right and inflation drops quickly, which is what happened to UK inflation in 2023–24 as energy price effects dropped out of the annual comparison. If higher prices are permanent, some energy-intensive production becomes unviable and LRAS may shift left, reducing potential output.

Overall, a sustained energy price shock is very likely to raise the price level and reduce real output in the short run. The most important factor in determining the long-run damage is whether it triggers second-round wage effects; with credible monetary policy and temporary fiscal support, the UK experience suggests the inflationary effect can be contained within two to three years, but the loss of real income is not recovered quickly.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: clear definition of equilibrium and correct identification of a cost-push SRAS shift, with accurate diagram labels. Application: detailed and accurate UK 2022 data, Energy Price Guarantee and Bank Rate path. Analysis: SRAS shift, additional AD effects through real incomes and investment, and second-round wage-price effects. Evaluation: energy intensity, fiscal response, monetary response and duration of the shock, prioritised to reach a justified judgement. This reaches Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation for 12 marks.

title: The multiplier
overview: The multiplier is the process by which an initial change in an injection (or withdrawal) causes a larger final change in national income, because one person's spending becomes another's income and is partly re-spent. Its size depends on the marginal propensities to save, tax and import. Edexcel examines the multiplier through calculations (multiplier ratio, MPC, MPW) and through evaluation of fiscal policy, investment and export shocks, so you need both precise arithmetic and judgement about its real-world size.
objectives: Explain the multiplier process round by round using the circular flow
Define and calculate MPC, MPS, MPT, MPM and MPW, and the multiplier ratio
Calculate the final change in national income from a change in an injection, and the injection needed to close a gap
Show the multiplier on an AD/AS diagram, including the negative multiplier
Evaluate the significance of the multiplier for government policy and the UK economy

sections.heading: The multiplier process
sections.body:
The **multiplier effect** is the process by which an initial change in an injection leads to a proportionately larger final change in national income.

Suppose the government spends an extra £10bn building new hospitals. Construction firms receive £10bn of revenue, which they pay out as wages, profits and payments to suppliers, so national income has risen by £10bn in round one. The recipients do not withdraw all of this: they spend part of it on UK goods and services, perhaps £6bn. That £6bn becomes income for shopkeepers, restaurant workers and their employers (round two). They in turn spend 60% of it, £3.6bn (round three), and so on.

With 40% withdrawn and 60% re-spent at each round:

- Round 1: income rises £10bn; £4bn is withdrawn and £6bn re-spent.
- Round 2: income rises £6bn; £2.4bn withdrawn, £3.6bn re-spent.
- Round 3: income rises £3.6bn; £1.44bn withdrawn, £2.16bn re-spent.
- Round 4: income rises £2.16bn; about £0.86bn withdrawn, £1.30bn re-spent.
- And so on, until the rounds become negligible. In total income rises £25bn, of which £10bn is withdrawn.

Each round is smaller because of **withdrawals**: at every stage some income is saved, taxed or spent on imports. The process ends when the total extra withdrawals equal the original injection (£10bn), which is exactly the condition for a new equilibrium (J = W). The sum of the rounds is £25bn, so the multiplier is 25 ÷ 10 = **2.5**.

The multiplier works in **both directions**. A fall in an injection, such as a collapse in exports or a cut in public investment, reduces national income by a multiple of the initial fall: the **negative multiplier**. This is why recessions can deepen rapidly.

sections.heading: Marginal propensities and the multiplier ratio
sections.body:
The size of the multiplier depends on how much of each extra pound of income is passed on as spending on domestic output.

- **Marginal propensity to consume (MPC)** = ΔC ÷ ΔY: the proportion of an extra pound of income spent on domestic output.
- **Marginal propensity to save (MPS)** = ΔS ÷ ΔY.
- **Marginal propensity to tax (MPT)** = ΔT ÷ ΔY: the proportion of an extra pound of income paid in taxes.
- **Marginal propensity to import (MPM)** = ΔM ÷ ΔY.
- **Marginal propensity to withdraw (MPW)** = MPS + MPT + MPM.

Every extra pound is either passed on or withdrawn, so **MPC + MPW = 1** (using MPC to mean spending on domestic output out of gross income).

The **multiplier ratio** is:

**k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPW = 1 ÷ (MPS + MPT + MPM)**

and the final change in national income is **ΔY = k × ΔJ** (the change in the injection).

The intuition: the larger the share of income that leaks out at each round, the faster the rounds shrink and the smaller the multiplier. In a simple closed economy without government, MPC might be 0.8 and k = 5; once realistic taxes and imports are included, k is much smaller. An open economy with high taxes has a small multiplier. Note that the multiplier ratio is derived from **marginal** propensities (behaviour at the margin), not average propensities (total consumption ÷ total income).

sections.heading: Worked calculations
sections.body:
**Example 1: multiplier from withdrawal propensities.** MPS = 0.1, MPT = 0.2, MPM = 0.3. MPW = 0.6, so k = 1 ÷ 0.6 = **1.67**. A £12bn rise in investment raises national income by 12 × 1.67 = **£20bn**.

**Example 2: from MPC.** Households spend 75p of every extra pound of gross income on UK output. MPC = 0.75, so k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = **4**.

**Example 3: calculating MPC from data.** When national income rises from £800bn to £850bn, consumption of domestic output rises from £500bn to £530bn. MPC = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6, so k = 1 ÷ 0.4 = **2.5**. Note the average propensity to consume is 530 ÷ 850 ≈ 0.62, which is not used.

**Example 4: closing an output gap.** Real GDP is £40bn below potential and k = 1.6. The injection needed is ΔJ = ΔY ÷ k = 40 ÷ 1.6 = **£25bn**.

**Example 5: finding the multiplier from outcomes.** Exports fall by £15bn and national income falls by £24bn. k = 24 ÷ 15 = **1.6**, so MPW = 1 ÷ 1.6 = **0.625**.

**Example 6: change in a propensity.** If MPT rises from 0.2 to 0.3 (MPS = 0.1, MPM = 0.3), MPW rises from 0.6 to 0.7 and k falls from 1.67 to 1.43. Higher tax rates, or a rising share of imports, make the economy less responsive to injections, which is a key point when evaluating fiscal policy.

Always show the formula, substitution and units (£bn); method marks are available even if arithmetic slips.

sections.heading: Showing the multiplier on an AD/AS diagram
sections.body:
On an AD/AS diagram an increase in an injection first shifts AD from AD1 to AD2 by the amount of the injection. The multiplier then shifts AD further, to AD3, so the total horizontal shift is k times the initial injection.

Notice what the diagram reveals. Because SRAS slopes upward, part of the extra demand raises the **price level** rather than real output. The increase in **real** national output (Y1 to Y3) is smaller than the horizontal shift of AD. The closer the economy is to full capacity, the steeper the AS curve and the more the multiplied increase in demand is absorbed by inflation rather than growth. At full capacity, the real multiplier is close to zero.

The diagram for the negative multiplier is the mirror image: a fall in exports shifts AD left initially, then further as incomes and spending fall, lowering real output and the price level (or the rate of inflation).

The multiplier also interacts with the **accelerator** (2.2.3). As national income rises, firms need more capacity, so investment rises, which is itself an injection that triggers further multiplier effects. Together the multiplier and accelerator help explain why booms and recessions build momentum, as seen in the trade cycle (2.5.3).

sections.heading: The significance of the multiplier
sections.body:
The multiplier matters because it tells policymakers how much national income will change following a shock or a policy decision.

- **Fiscal policy**: if k is large, a modest rise in G or cut in taxes can close a negative output gap, and fiscal stimulus partly pays for itself through higher tax revenues. If k is small, fiscal policy is weak and expensive. The OBR uses multipliers in its forecasts: it has assumed that public investment has a multiplier of roughly 1, while most tax changes have multipliers well below 1, partly because some of a tax cut is saved.
- **Austerity**: a large multiplier implies that cutting government spending reduces GDP significantly, possibly worsening the debt-to-GDP ratio. In 2013 IMF economists suggested that forecasters had underestimated fiscal multipliers during the post-2008 consolidation in Europe, which helped explain weaker-than-forecast growth.
- **Regional policy**: a new factory or major infrastructure project can have multiplier effects on a local area, though local multipliers are smaller because much spending leaks to other regions.
- **External shocks**: a fall in demand for UK exports from a recession in the EU or US is magnified through the multiplier.

**Limitations of the multiplier as a guide:**

- Propensities are **not constant**. In a recession, uncertain households save more of any extra income (higher MPS), so the multiplier is smaller just when it is needed.
- **Time lags**: the rounds take months or years to work through; the full effect is not immediate.
- **Crowding out**: if extra government borrowing raises interest rates, private investment may fall, offsetting the injection (more likely near full capacity, less so with spare capacity and low rates).
- **Monetary policy offset**: if fiscal stimulus raises inflation risk, the Bank of England may raise Bank Rate, reducing the net effect.
- **Capacity**: with no spare capacity the multiplier raises prices, not real output.
- **Estimation**: the multiplier cannot be observed directly; estimates for the UK vary widely, commonly between about 0.5 and 1.5 depending on the policy and the state of the economy.

The final change in national income divided by the initial change in an injection: k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPW.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that is spent on domestic consumption: ΔC ÷ ΔY.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that is saved: ΔS ÷ ΔY.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that is paid in taxation: ΔT ÷ ΔY.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that is spent on imports: ΔM ÷ ΔY.
The proportion of an additional pound of income that leaks out of the circular flow: MPS + MPT + MPM = 1 − MPC.
The process by which a fall in an injection or a rise in a withdrawal causes a proportionately larger fall in national income.
The change in GDP resulting from a change in government spending or taxation, divided by the size of the policy change.
The reduction in private sector spending, especially investment, that may result when increased government borrowing raises interest rates or absorbs resources.
The theory that the level of net investment depends on the rate of change of national income, so faster growth raises investment.

diagrams.title: The multiplier effect on AD
diagrams.caption: An injection first shifts AD1 to AD2 (initial effect, ΔJ). Induced consumption shifts AD further to AD3, a total shift of k × ΔJ (here k = 2.5). Because SRAS slopes upward, real output rises from Y1 to Y3, by less than the horizontal shift, and the price level rises from P1 to P3.

diagrams.title: The negative multiplier
diagrams.caption: A fall in exports or investment shifts AD1 to AD2 initially; falling incomes reduce consumption and AD falls further to AD3. Real output falls from Y1 to Y3 and the price level from P1 to P3 (in practice, inflation slows).

formulae.name: Multiplier ratio
formulae.formula: k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPW

formulae.name: Marginal propensity to withdraw
formulae.formula: MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM

formulae.name: Final change in national income
formulae.formula: ΔY = k × ΔJ
formulae.example: k = 1.67 and a £12bn rise in investment: ΔY = 1.67 × 12 ≈ £20bn.

formulae.name: Injection needed to close a gap
formulae.formula: ΔJ = ΔY ÷ k
formulae.example: A £40bn negative output gap with k = 1.6 requires an injection of 40 ÷ 1.6 = £25bn.

formulae.name: Marginal propensity to consume
formulae.formula: MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY
formulae.example: Income rises £50bn and domestic consumption rises £30bn: MPC = 0.6.

applications: Public investment: the 2024 change in the UK's debt measure for the fiscal rules (to public sector net financial liabilities) was justified partly by the argument that capital spending has a relatively high multiplier and raises potential output, so it should not be treated the same as day-to-day spending.

Post-2008 austerity: research by IMF economists in 2013 argued that fiscal multipliers during the European consolidation were larger than forecasters had assumed, often above 1 rather than around 0.5, because interest rates were already near zero and many economies had spare capacity. This helps explain why austerity reduced growth more than expected.

Regional multipliers: large projects such as a new car battery gigafactory or a freeport bring local multiplier effects through suppliers and workers' spending, but much of the income leaks out of the region through imports, national taxes and spending elsewhere in the UK.

Open economies: in small, highly open economies such as Ireland or the Netherlands, imports are a very large share of GDP, so the MPM is high and fiscal multipliers are small; the US, with imports a much smaller share of GDP, has a larger multiplier for a given policy.
evaluation: The UK's high propensity to import and relatively high marginal tax rates mean MPW is large and the multiplier is modest; part of any stimulus raises demand for foreign output.

The multiplier is state-dependent: larger in a deep recession with spare capacity and interest rates near zero (little crowding out or monetary offset), smaller near full capacity, where it raises prices rather than real output.
Confidence and expectations: households may save tax cuts if they expect future tax rises to repay debt (Ricardian equivalence) or if they fear unemployment, reducing the multiplier.
The composition of spending matters: capital spending and transfers to low-income households (higher MPC) tend to have larger multipliers than tax cuts for high earners (higher MPS).
Time lags mean the full effect may arrive after the economy has already recovered, risking pro-cyclical stimulus.
Multipliers are estimates with wide ranges; policy based on a precise figure is risky, so a judgement should be framed as 'likely' rather than certain.
misconceptions: Using average propensities (total C ÷ total Y) instead of marginal propensities in the multiplier formula.
Writing k = 1 ÷ MPC. The correct ratio is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), equivalently 1 ÷ MPW.
Assuming the full multiplied shift in AD becomes extra real output. With upward-sloping AS, part is absorbed by a higher price level.
Thinking the multiplier only works for government spending. Any change in an injection (I, X) or in the propensity to withdraw has multiplier effects, including negative ones.
Forgetting that a larger MPS, MPT or MPM makes the multiplier smaller, not larger.
exam_tips: Calculation questions are common in Section A: write the formula, substitute, and give the answer with units. If asked for the change in income, multiply k by the injection.

In essays on fiscal policy, use the multiplier to explain why the effect on GDP is larger than the initial spending, then evaluate its size using UK leakages (especially imports) and the state of the economy.
Draw the multiplier as two AD shifts (initial and final) and point out that real output rises by less than the AD shift because of the slope of AS.
Link the multiplier to the accelerator and trade cycle for synoptic credit.
When data show propensities, check whether MPC is given out of disposable or gross income; for the ratio 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) to equal 1 ÷ MPW, all propensities must be out of the same income measure.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the significance of the multiplier effect for the success of an increase in UK government capital spending designed to raise economic growth.
model_answer.answer:
Government capital spending is investment by the state in infrastructure such as transport, hospitals and energy networks. It is an injection into the circular flow and a component of AD. The multiplier effect is the process by which an initial injection leads to a proportionately larger final change in national income, because the income received by one group is partly re-spent and becomes income for others. The multiplier ratio is k = 1 ÷ MPW, where MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM.

Suppose the government spends an extra £20bn on rail and energy infrastructure. Construction firms and their suppliers receive £20bn, which is paid out as wages and profits. Recipients spend part of it on UK goods and services, creating income for retailers, hospitality and manufacturers, who in turn spend part of their extra income. If MPS = 0.1, MPT = 0.25 and MPM = 0.25, MPW = 0.6 and k is about 1.67, so national income rises by around £33bn. On an AD/AS diagram, AD shifts from AD1 to AD2 by the initial £20bn and then on to AD3 as induced consumption rises. Real output increases from Y1 to Y3 and, because firms now expect higher sales, the accelerator may raise private investment, a further injection with its own multiplier effect. The multiplier therefore makes the policy more powerful and partly self-financing, since higher incomes raise tax revenues.

Capital spending is distinctive because it also raises long-run aggregate supply. Better transport links reduce firms' costs and widen labour markets; investment in grid capacity supports new energy supply. LRAS shifts right, so the growth is more sustainable and less inflationary than a rise in current spending.

However, the significance of the multiplier depends on several factors. First, the UK has a high propensity to import: much construction equipment, materials and consumer goods are imported, so leakages are large and the domestic multiplier may be close to 1 rather than 1.67. The OBR has assumed a multiplier of roughly 1 for public investment. Second, it depends on spare capacity. If the economy is close to full capacity, as indicated by low unemployment and labour shortages in construction, the multiplied rise in AD mainly raises costs and the price level rather than real output, and the Bank of England may respond by keeping Bank Rate higher, offsetting the stimulus. Third, crowding out: if the spending is financed by borrowing at a time when gilt yields are high, as they were after 2022, higher debt interest costs and possibly higher interest rates may reduce private investment. Fourth, time lags are long: major projects such as HS2 have taken many years to plan and build and faced large cost overruns, so the AD effect is delayed and the supply-side benefits further still. Finally, the effect depends on project quality: poorly chosen projects have low long-run returns even if they have short-run multiplier effects.

Overall, the multiplier is significant because it means capital spending raises GDP by more than its direct cost in the short run, especially when there is spare capacity and interest rates are low. But in the UK the multiplier is probably modest because of high import and tax leakages, and the more important determinant of success is the supply-side return on the projects. The policy is most likely to succeed if spending is well targeted, delivered without long delays and timed when the economy has a negative output gap.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions and correct multiplier formula. Application: illustrative calculation, OBR multiplier assumption, gilt yields, HS2, UK import propensity. Analysis: chain through rounds of spending, AD shifts with diagram reference, accelerator, self-financing through tax revenue, and supply-side effects on LRAS. Evaluation: leakages, spare capacity and monetary offset, crowding out, time lags and project quality, with a weighted final judgement identifying the most important factor. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation for 15 marks.
