title: Conflicts and trade-offs
overview: Macroeconomic objectives often conflict: policies that boost growth and employment can raise inflation and worsen the current account, while policies that cut inflation or the budget deficit can raise unemployment. This topic analyses the main trade-offs, the short-run and long-run Phillips curves, and how policymakers have handled conflicts in historical episodes such as the Great Depression, the 1970s, the 1980s, the Great Recession and the 2022 inflation surge. It provides the core evaluation for almost every Theme 2 essay and is heavily used in Paper 2 and Paper 3 25-mark questions.
objectives: Explain the main potential conflicts between macroeconomic objectives in the short run and the long run
Draw and explain the short-run Phillips curve and the trade-off between unemployment and inflation
Draw and explain the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, the vertical long-run Phillips curve and the NAIRU
Evaluate the evidence on the Phillips curve in the UK, including the 1970s and recent experience
Evaluate how policymakers have managed trade-offs in historical episodes, including the Great Depression and the Great Recession

sections.heading: Why objectives conflict
sections.body:
Demand-side policies shift AD, and an AD shift moves output, employment, the price level and the current account **at the same time**. Pursuing one objective therefore often affects others, in the wrong direction. The main conflicts:

- **Growth and low unemployment versus low inflation.** Raising AD increases real output and reduces unemployment, but as the economy approaches capacity, the price level rises (demand-pull inflation). Conversely, raising Bank Rate to cut inflation reduces AD, slowing growth and raising unemployment.
- **Growth versus the current account.** Rising incomes increase imports (the UK has a high marginal propensity to import), and domestic inflation reduces competitiveness, so fast growth tends to widen the current account deficit.
- **Growth versus the environment.** Higher output generally increases resource use and emissions unless growth is decoupled through cleaner technology and policy.
- **Growth versus equality.** Market-based supply-side policies, such as lower top tax rates or weaker employment protection, may raise incentives and growth but widen inequality; redistribution may weaken incentives.
- **Budget balance versus growth and employment.** Cutting the deficit through spending cuts or tax rises reduces AD, which can slow growth and raise unemployment, at least in the short run (the austerity debate after 2010).
- **Inflation versus the current account.** Higher interest rates tend to appreciate sterling, making exports dearer and imports cheaper, which worsens the current account even as it helps reduce inflation.
- **Supply shocks create the starkest conflict.** An adverse supply shock (SRAS shifts left) raises inflation and reduces output simultaneously; any demand-side response must sacrifice one objective for the other.

Many conflicts are **short-run**. In the long run, supply-side improvements can raise growth, reduce unemployment and lower inflation together.

sections.heading: The short-run Phillips curve
sections.body:
In 1958 the economist A.W. Phillips published a study of UK data from 1861 to 1957 showing an inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the rate of change of money wages. Because wage growth feeds into price inflation, this became the **Phillips curve**: a negative relationship between **unemployment and inflation**.

**Why the trade-off exists**: when AD is high, firms want to hire more workers. Unemployment falls, the labour market tightens and workers gain bargaining power, so firms bid up wages to attract and retain staff. Higher wages raise costs and are passed on as higher prices. When unemployment is high, workers have little bargaining power and wage growth slows.

The curve is **convex**: at very low unemployment, further falls in unemployment require large increases in inflation, because the labour market is near capacity; at high unemployment, extra unemployment does little to reduce inflation further.

In the 1950s and 1960s the Phillips curve appeared to offer policymakers a **menu of choices**: a government could choose lower unemployment by accepting somewhat higher inflation, using demand management to move along the curve. A movement from point A (high unemployment, low inflation) to point B (low unemployment, higher inflation) would be achieved by expanding AD.

On an AD/AS diagram, the same idea appears as AD moving along an upward-sloping SRAS: higher output (and employment) comes with a higher price level.

sections.heading: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve and the NAIRU
sections.body:
In the late 1960s Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that the trade-off was **only temporary**, because it ignored **inflation expectations**. Workers care about **real** wages. If they expect inflation of 2%, they will negotiate wage increases accordingly.

The process, starting at the **natural rate of unemployment** (or NAIRU) with 2% inflation (point A):

- The government expands AD to reduce unemployment below the NAIRU. Firms raise prices and hire more workers by offering higher money wages. Workers, still expecting 2% inflation, believe their real wages have risen and supply more labour. Unemployment falls and inflation rises to 4%: a movement along SRPC1 to point B.
- Workers realise prices are rising faster than they expected, so real wages have not risen. Expected inflation rises to 4% and workers demand higher money wages. The short-run Phillips curve shifts up to SRPC2.
- As real wages return to their previous level, firms reduce employment and unemployment returns to the NAIRU, but now with 4% inflation (point C).

The **long-run Phillips curve (LRPC)** is therefore **vertical at the NAIRU**. In the long run there is no trade-off: attempts to hold unemployment below the NAIRU lead to **accelerating** inflation. This mirrors the classical vertical LRAS.

**Policy implications**:

- Demand management cannot permanently reduce unemployment below the NAIRU; it can only stabilise around it.
- To reduce unemployment permanently, the NAIRU itself must be reduced through **supply-side policies** (better skills and matching, flexible labour markets, incentives to work).
- **Credibility** matters: if the central bank's inflation target is believed, expectations stay anchored at 2% and the short-run curve does not shift up, making disinflation less costly. This is a central argument for central bank independence.
- Reducing inflation once expectations are high requires unemployment above the NAIRU for a period (a movement down along the SRPC) until expectations fall.

sections.heading: The evidence: stagflation, disinflation and a flat Phillips curve
sections.body:
**1970s stagflation**: oil price shocks (1973–74 and 1979) and rising inflation expectations produced high inflation and rising unemployment simultaneously. UK inflation peaked at over 20% in 1975. The simple Phillips curve 'broke down', consistent with the SRPC shifting outward as expectations rose and with adverse supply shocks.

**1980s disinflation**: the Thatcher government and the Bank of England tightened policy sharply to bring inflation down. Inflation fell from around 18% in 1980 to under 5% by 1983, but unemployment rose above 3 million (over 11%), consistent with moving down a short-run Phillips curve while expectations adjusted. It illustrates the **sacrifice ratio**: the output and jobs lost to reduce inflation.

**The 'Great Moderation' and the flat Phillips curve**: from the 1990s, inflation targeting and later Bank of England independence anchored expectations near 2%. In the late 2010s UK unemployment fell to around 4% (its lowest since the mid-1970s) with inflation remaining close to target and wage growth subdued. The Phillips curve appeared **flat**. Explanations include anchored expectations, globalisation (cheap imports and international competition), weaker trade unions, more flexible and insecure work (zero-hours contracts, self-employment), and a fall in the NAIRU.

**2021–23**: as the labour market became extremely tight (vacancies above 1.3 million in 2022) and energy prices surged, inflation rose to 11.1% and wage growth accelerated, suggesting the Phillips curve became **steeper** again at very low unemployment, and that a combination of supply shocks and tight labour markets can de-anchor expectations. The MPC's concern about second-round effects (persistent wage and services inflation) explains why it kept Bank Rate high for an extended period.

sections.heading: Managing trade-offs: historical perspectives
sections.body:
**The Great Depression (1930s).** Governments prioritised balanced budgets and the gold standard (and so exchange rate stability) over employment. Spending cuts and tight money as output fell deepened the slump; US unemployment reached about 25% and UK unemployment rose to close to 3 million. Recovery came only when countries abandoned the gold standard, allowing lower interest rates, and later through large-scale spending. Lesson: prioritising budget balance and a fixed exchange rate in a deep recession worsens unemployment.

**Post-war demand management (1950s–60s)**: the UK prioritised full employment but repeatedly ran into the **balance of payments constraint**: booms sucked in imports, the current account worsened, and governments had to tighten policy ('stop-go'), sacrificing growth to protect sterling.

**The Great Recession (2008–09 onward)**: the MPC faced a conflict when CPI inflation rose above 3% (reaching around 5% in 2011, partly because of the VAT rise and higher import prices after sterling's fall) while unemployment was above 8%. It chose to 'look through' the temporary inflation, keeping Bank Rate at 0.5% and using QE to support output, judging that spare capacity would bring inflation down. Fiscal policy shifted from stimulus to **austerity** from 2010, prioritising the deficit; critics argue this slowed the recovery.

**2022–23**: with inflation far above target and the economy stagnating, the MPC prioritised inflation by raising Bank Rate to 5.25%, accepting weaker growth; the government's Energy Price Guarantee reduced measured inflation and protected incomes but increased borrowing, a conflict with the budget objective.

**Resolving conflicts**: policymakers can use a **policy mix**: assigning monetary policy to inflation, fiscal policy to stabilisation and the public finances over the medium term, and supply-side policy to growth and the NAIRU. Supply-side improvements shift LRAS (and the LRPC) to the right, reducing the conflict. Temporary, targeted measures (such as the Energy Price Guarantee) can ease trade-offs in the short run.

key_terms.definition: A situation in which pursuing one macroeconomic objective makes it harder to achieve another, such as reducing inflation at the cost of higher unemployment.
A curve showing an inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the rate of inflation (originally the rate of change of money wages).
The downward-sloping relationship between unemployment and inflation for a given level of expected inflation.
A vertical line at the natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU), showing no long-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation once expectations adjust.
The non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment: the rate of unemployment at which inflation is stable, with no tendency to accelerate or decelerate.
The rate of unemployment when the labour market is in equilibrium, consisting of frictional and structural unemployment; associated with the vertical LRPC.
The rate of inflation that households, workers and firms expect in the future, which influences wage bargaining and price setting.
The simultaneous occurrence of high inflation and high or rising unemployment with stagnant output.
The cumulative loss of output (or rise in unemployment) required to reduce inflation by one percentage point.
The combination of monetary, fiscal and supply-side policies used to pursue several objectives at once.
The limit on growth that arises when faster growth causes an unsustainable current account deficit, forcing policy to be tightened.

diagrams.title: Short-run Phillips curve
diagrams.caption: Expanding AD moves the economy from A to B: unemployment falls from U1 to U2 but inflation rises from π1 to π2. The curve is convex, so cutting unemployment further costs ever more inflation.

diagrams.title: Expectations-augmented Phillips curve and the NAIRU
diagrams.caption: Expansion moves the economy from A to B on SRPC1. When expected inflation rises to 4%, SRPC shifts up to SRPC2 and unemployment returns to the NAIRU at C, with higher inflation. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the NAIRU.

diagrams.title: Conflict: higher AD raises output and the price level
diagrams.caption: Expansionary policy raises output from Y1 to Y2 (higher growth, lower unemployment) but raises the price level from P1 to P2, and rising incomes increase imports: growth and employment conflict with inflation and the current account.

diagrams.title: Supply shock: the starkest conflict
diagrams.caption: An adverse supply shock raises the price level (P1 to P2) and reduces output (Y1 to Y2). Tightening policy to fight inflation deepens the fall in output; loosening to protect output adds to inflation.

formulae.name: Expectations-augmented Phillips curve (simplified)
formulae.formula: Inflation = expected inflation − b × (unemployment − NAIRU)
formulae.example: Expected inflation 2%, b = 0.8, NAIRU 4.5%, unemployment 3.5%: inflation = 2 − 0.8 × (3.5 − 4.5) = 2.8%.

formulae.name: Sacrifice ratio
formulae.formula: Sacrifice ratio = cumulative % output lost ÷ percentage-point fall in inflation
formulae.example: Cutting inflation from 8% to 2% at a cumulative loss of 9% of GDP: sacrifice ratio = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5.

formulae.name: Misery index (informal indicator)
formulae.formula: Misery index = inflation rate + unemployment rate
formulae.example: Inflation 6.7% and unemployment 4.2%: misery index 10.9.

applications: 1970s UK stagflation: following the 1973–74 oil shock and rapid wage growth, inflation peaked at over 20% in 1975 while unemployment rose, undermining belief in a stable Phillips curve trade-off and paving the way for monetarist ideas.

Early 1980s disinflation: tight monetary and fiscal policy reduced UK inflation from around 18% in 1980 to under 5% by 1983, but unemployment rose above 3 million, illustrating the short-run cost of reducing inflation once expectations are high.
Late 2010s: UK unemployment fell to around 4% in 2019, the lowest since the mid-1970s, while CPI inflation stayed close to 2%, consistent with a flat Phillips curve and anchored expectations.

2022–23: CPI inflation of 11.1% with a very tight labour market led the MPC to raise Bank Rate to 5.25%, accepting near-zero growth in 2023 and rising unemployment in 2024–25 to bring inflation down: a clear inflation versus growth trade-off.

Post-2010 austerity: prioritising deficit reduction while the economy had spare capacity is widely debated; critics argue it slowed the recovery (budget versus growth conflict), while supporters argue it maintained credibility and low borrowing costs.

US 1980s: the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker raised interest rates to very high levels to break double-digit inflation, causing a recession in 1981–82 with unemployment close to 11%, after which inflation stayed low for decades.
evaluation: Many conflicts are short-run: in the long run, supply-side improvements can raise growth, reduce the NAIRU and lower inflation together, so the trade-off depends on the time horizon.
The size of the trade-off depends on the slope of the Phillips curve and SRAS, which vary with spare capacity, expectations and globalisation; it was flat in the 2010s and steeper in 2021–22.

The type of shock matters: demand shocks move output and inflation in the same direction, so there is no conflict in stabilising them; supply shocks move them in opposite directions, creating a genuine dilemma.
Credibility reduces trade-offs: an independent central bank with anchored expectations can reduce inflation with a smaller rise in unemployment (lower sacrifice ratio).
The NAIRU is uncertain and shifts over time, so policymakers cannot be sure where the vertical LRPC lies; acting on a wrong estimate creates errors.
Which objective to prioritise involves value judgements about who bears the cost: unemployment falls heavily on particular groups, while inflation affects those on fixed incomes and savers.
A well-designed policy mix and targeted measures can reduce, but rarely eliminate, conflicts in the short run.
misconceptions: Believing the Phillips curve offers a permanent menu of choices. With adaptive expectations, the trade-off is only temporary; the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
Drawing the LRPC at zero unemployment. It is vertical at the NAIRU (natural rate), which is positive.
Thinking a supply shock moves the economy along the Phillips curve. It shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward (more inflation at each unemployment rate).
Assuming all objectives always conflict. Demand-led recessions reduce growth and inflation together, so stimulus helps both employment and the inflation target if inflation is below 2%.
Confusing the trade-off between unemployment and inflation with the trade-off between growth and the current account; explain the specific mechanism for each.
exam_tips: Draw both Phillips curve diagrams accurately: convex SRPC, vertical LRPC at the NAIRU, shifting SRPC as expectations change. Label axes 'Unemployment (%)' and 'Inflation (%)'.
In 25-mark essays, explicitly identify the conflict, explain its mechanism with a diagram, then evaluate using time horizon, type of shock, credibility and supply-side policy.
Use historical episodes (1930s, 1970s, 1980s, 2008, 2022) to support evaluation; the specification expects a historical perspective on policy.
Link to AD/AS: a movement along the SRPC corresponds to AD moving along SRAS; the vertical LRPC corresponds to vertical LRAS.
Show awareness that the Phillips curve has flattened and steepened at different times, rather than treating it as a fixed law.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that there is an unavoidable trade-off between reducing unemployment and keeping inflation low in the UK.
model_answer.answer:
The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. A.W. Phillips found that between 1861 and 1957, UK wage growth was faster when unemployment was low. The view in the question is that policymakers can only reduce unemployment by accepting higher inflation, and only reduce inflation by accepting higher unemployment.

There is a clear mechanism behind the short-run trade-off. If the government or the Bank of England expands aggregate demand, for example by cutting Bank Rate or raising government spending, firms increase output and hire more workers, because labour is a derived demand. As unemployment falls, the labour market tightens, workers' bargaining power increases and firms must offer higher wages to recruit and retain staff. Higher wages raise unit labour costs, which firms pass on in higher prices. On a short-run Phillips curve diagram, the economy moves from point A, with higher unemployment and low inflation, to point B, with lower unemployment and higher inflation. On an AD/AS diagram, AD shifts right along an upward-sloping SRAS, raising real output and the price level together. The convex shape of the curve means that as unemployment approaches very low levels, further reductions cost increasingly large rises in inflation.

UK evidence supports a short-run trade-off. In the early 1980s, tight monetary and fiscal policy reduced inflation from around 18% to under 5% in three years, but unemployment rose above 3 million. More recently, in 2022–23, the MPC raised Bank Rate from 0.1% to 5.25% to bring inflation down from 11.1%; growth stagnated and unemployment drifted up in 2024–25. Conversely, in 2021–22 the very tight labour market, with vacancies above 1.3 million, coincided with rapid wage growth and rising services inflation.

However, the trade-off is not unavoidable in the long run. Friedman and Phelps argued that the trade-off exists only while inflation expectations are unchanged. If unemployment is held below the NAIRU, workers realise their real wages have not risen, expected inflation rises, and the short-run Phillips curve shifts up. Unemployment returns to the NAIRU at a higher inflation rate. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the NAIRU, so demand management cannot permanently reduce unemployment; it can only change inflation. The 1970s, when UK inflation exceeded 20% in 1975 while unemployment rose, show what happens when expectations become de-anchored.

This means the trade-off can be avoided by reducing the NAIRU itself. Supply-side policies that improve skills, health and job matching, reduce barriers to work and improve incentives shift the long-run Phillips curve to the left, allowing lower unemployment without higher inflation. Interventionist policies addressing the UK's high economic inactivity due to long-term sickness and skills shortages, and the expansion of childcare support, could increase effective labour supply and ease wage pressure at a given unemployment rate.

The trade-off can also be weakened by credibility. Since the 1990s, inflation targeting and Bank of England independence have anchored expectations close to 2%. In the late 2010s unemployment fell to around 4%, the lowest since the 1970s, while inflation stayed close to target: the Phillips curve appeared almost flat. Globalisation, cheaper imports and weaker union bargaining power also made wages less responsive to unemployment. In this environment, lower unemployment came with little inflation cost.

The nature of the shock is crucial. When inflation is caused by a fall in AD, there is no conflict: stimulus raises employment and brings inflation back up towards target, as in 2009–2013. When inflation is caused by an adverse supply shock, as in 2022, there is a genuine dilemma, because inflation and unemployment rise together; any attempt to cut inflation further reduces output and employment. The trade-off was therefore much sharper in 2022 than in the 2010s.

Finally, the slope of the curve varies. The 2021–23 experience suggests the Phillips curve becomes much steeper when the labour market is very tight, so the trade-off is not stable, and estimates of the NAIRU are uncertain, making it difficult for the MPC to know exactly where the long-run curve lies.

Overall, there is an unavoidable short-run trade-off when the economy is close to full capacity or hit by a supply shock, and policymakers must then decide which objective to prioritise. But the trade-off is not unavoidable in the long run: credible monetary policy keeps it shallow by anchoring expectations, and supply-side policies can lower the NAIRU so that the UK can enjoy lower unemployment and low inflation together. The most important determinant is whether expectations remain anchored; if they do, the cost of keeping inflation low is modest, as in the 2010s; if they do not, as in the 1970s, the trade-off becomes very costly.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: accurate account of the Phillips curve, its origins, the expectations-augmented model, the NAIRU and the vertical LRPC. Application: well-chosen UK evidence from the 1970s, early 1980s, 2010s and 2021–25. Analysis: clear chains for the short-run trade-off and the long-run adjustment, linked to AD/AS and both Phillips curve diagrams. Evaluation: long-run versus short-run, supply-side reduction of the NAIRU, credibility and anchored expectations, the type of shock and the changing slope of the curve, culminating in a supported judgement identifying the key determinant. This would reach Level 4 KAA (13–16) and Level 3 evaluation (7–9) for 25 marks.

check.q: According to the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, what is the long-run effect of using demand-side policy to hold unemployment below the NAIRU?
options: Permanently lower unemployment with stable inflation
Accelerating inflation with unemployment eventually returning to the NAIRU
Falling inflation and rising unemployment
No change in inflation or unemployment
check.explanation: As expectations adjust, the SRPC shifts up repeatedly; holding unemployment below the NAIRU requires ever-rising inflation.

check.q: The long-run Phillips curve is:
options: Downward sloping and convex
Vertical at the natural rate of unemployment
Horizontal at the inflation target
Vertical at zero unemployment
check.explanation: With fully adjusted expectations there is no long-run trade-off; the LRPC is vertical at the NAIRU.

check.q: Which event best illustrates stagflation?
options: UK in the late 2010s
UK in 1975
UK in 2009
UK in the 1950s
check.explanation: In 1975 UK inflation peaked above 20% while unemployment was rising, after the oil price shock.

check.q: Which policy is most likely to reduce unemployment without increasing inflation in the long run?
options: Cut in Bank Rate
Increase in government current spending
Policies that improve skills and job matching, lowering the NAIRU
Depreciation of sterling
check.explanation: Supply-side policies shift the LRPC left by reducing the NAIRU; the others raise AD, which in the long run mainly raises inflation.

check.q: Raising Bank Rate to reduce inflation is most likely to conflict with which objective, via the exchange rate?
options: Lower budget deficit
Current account improvement
Environmental protection
Lower inflation
check.explanation: Higher rates tend to appreciate sterling, making exports dearer and imports cheaper, which worsens the current account.
